6.5 Swelling extent vs. initial cell size and survival¶

Left: does the magnitude of swelling depend on initial cell volume? Each dot is one frame-0 track; the x-axis is V(0), the y-axis is the maximum V(t)/V(0) reached during that track's lifetime.

Right: do cells that disappear (lyse) swell differently from those that survive? Population-averaged V(t)/V(0) curves split by outcome.

Why disappeared cells show lower median max swelling but higher curves at late frames: Disappeared cells burst early — many leave by frame 10-15 and had fewer frames to accumulate volume, so their lifetime peak is lower. The right panel shows the opposite at late frames because of survivorship bias: the only disappeared cells still tracked at frames 20+ are the extreme swellers that haven't burst yet. Both views are correct — they measure different things (lifetime peak vs. instantaneous population mean).

A more comparable metric is swelling rate per frame (printed below), which normalizes for lifetime differences.

8.3 Fluorescence vs. swelling correlation¶

Does fluorescence intensity track with cell volume? Each point is one cell at one frame. A positive correlation suggests fluorescence scales with cell size (membrane or cytoplasmic stain); no correlation suggests a localized signal (e.g., nuclear).

Source: tracked_cells.csv

8.4 Nucleoid heterogeneity: CV dynamics¶

CV (coefficient of variation = std/mean of pixel intensities within each cell mask) measures nucleoid spatial concentration. High CV = bright nucleoid spots on dark cytoplasmic background (intact, concentrated). Low CV = more uniform distribution (dispersed nucleoid).

Three views: absolute per frame, lifespan-normalized (all tracks aligned to [0,1]), and disappeared vs survived.

CV at frame 0: 0.486
CV at frame 30: 0.419

Sources: tracked_cells.csv, track_statistics.csv

8.4c Nucleoid edge-distance dynamics¶

Mean distance of suprathreshold fluorescence pixels from the cell-mask edge, normalized by R/3 (the expected mean-edge-distance for points uniformly distributed inside a circle of radius R). Values > 1 ⇒ pixels clustered toward the center; values < 1 ⇒ pixels at the periphery ("horseshoe"). Approaches 1 as the nucleoid disperses with swelling.

Edge-dist / (R/3) at frame 0: 1.544
Edge-dist / (R/3) at frame 30: 1.542

Sources: tracked_cells.csv, track_statistics.csv

8.5 Non-Normality Index (nNRM) dynamics¶

nNRM = Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic comparing pixel intensity distribution against a Gaussian with matching mean and std (Gough et al. 2014, PLOS ONE). Range [0, 1]: 0 = Gaussian, 1 = maximally non-Gaussian. Complements CV — CV measures spread, nNRM measures distribution shape. A high nNRM indicates distinct subpopulations within the cell mask (bright nucleoid vs dark cytoplasm).

nNRM at frame 0: 0.095
nNRM at frame 30: 0.087

Sources: tracked_cells.csv, track_statistics.csv

8.5b Nucleoid spatial σ dynamics¶

σ of the 2D intensity-weighted spatial distribution of suprathreshold pixels (mean of eigenvalues of the weighted covariance), normalized by the cell's pixel-space R. Captures dispersion: small σ ⇒ tight cluster; large σ ⇒ spread across the cell.

σ / R at frame 0: 0.339
σ / R at frame 30: 0.350

Sources: tracked_cells.csv, track_statistics.csv

8.5c Peri/core asymmetry dynamics¶

Signed asymmetry index (I_peri − I_core) / (I_peri + I_core) where the two regions are set by PERI_CORE_RINGS = (core_max, peri_min, peri_max) as fractions of the cell's equivalent radius R. Default (0.15, 0.35, 0.55) — narrow core samples the donut center dip, peri brackets the donut peak zone identified from real radial profiles (see docs/peri_core_asymmetry_definition_history.md for the sweep and the historical parameter sets). The intermediate band and the outer rim are ignored. Bounded in [−1, 1]:

  • positive → edge-clustered (expanded / donut-shaped nucleoid),
  • negative → center-clustered (compacted nucleoid),
  • 0 → radially uniform.

Areas are unequal, so mean rather than total intensity is used in each ring. Uses raw (unthresholded) intensities so the metric is defined even for near-uniform cells. Complements §8.4c (edge distance) and §8.5b (σ) — same three-panel layout by fate.

Peri/core asymmetry at frame 0: -0.043
Peri/core asymmetry at frame 30: -0.052

Sources: tracked_cells.csv, track_statistics.csv

8.5d Peri/core asymmetry aligned to phase disappearance¶

Per-cell trajectory of peri_core_asymmetry in the window [-FLUOR_ALIGN_WINDOW, 0] frames before each disappeared cell's last detection. Complements §8.5c by removing the averaging-across-frames artifact: cells caught at absolute frame N are at different stages of their own life cycle, so a per-frame median smears the trajectory. Aligning by offset from last-detected frame puts every cell on the same timeline relative to burst.

  • Left panel: individual trajectories (thin blue), median + IQR band across cells. Shows whether initial donut/sparse phenotypes converge to a common pre-burst state.
  • Right panel: baseline (offset -N) vs. last-frame (offset 0) scatter, one dot per cell. Points off the diagonal indicate a transformation between initial and pre-burst states.

8.6 Fluorescence dynamics around phase disappearance¶

Fluorescence loss is rarely instantaneous and rarely aligned with the phase mask vanishing — DNA exits through membrane pores more slowly than proteins, and the lysis itself can take multiple frames. To make this visible, for each disappeared cell we align its mean intensity to its last phase-detection frame and plot the ±FLUOR_ALIGN_WINDOW frames around that anchor.

Post-disappearance frames (offset > 0) use the cell's final phase mask to integrate fluorescence — the cell's last known ROI applied to subsequent fluorescence frames.

8.9 Fluorescence concentration (dilution-corrected)¶

Raw fluorescence intensity confounds true signal changes with dilution from cell swelling — a cell that doubles in volume halves its concentration even if total fluorophore content stays constant. Fluorescence concentration (total_intensity / volume) corrects for this, revealing whether fluorescence changes are biological or geometric.

Fluorescence concentration: 4960/4960 cells computed

Frame 30 mean concentration: 261399.030
Change: 0.58x

Source: tracked_cells.csv

8.11 Surface-area-to-volume ratio¶

SA:V ratio is a proxy for membrane mechanical stress. As cells swell (volume increases faster than surface area for a sphere), SA:V decreases — the membrane must stretch to accommodate the growing volume. Lower SA:V may indicate cells closer to their mechanical rupture threshold.

SA:V ratio: 4960/4960 cells computed

Does fluorescence change in the frames immediately before a cell disappears? For each disappeared track, fits a linear trend to mean fluorescence intensity in a 5-frame window before the last detection. A positive slope with intensity exceeding baseline indicates a pre-burst "spike" — possible membrane permeabilization allowing dye influx before final rupture.

8.14 Cell fate prediction from frame-0 features¶

Can we predict which cells will die just from their appearance at frame 0? Two complementary tests on the frame-0 cohort (cells visible at frame == 0, labelled by their eventual disappeared flag from track_statistics.csv):

  1. Univariate (next cell below). add_frame0_fate_comparison() runs a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test on area, cv, nnrm, mean_edge_distance_norm, and gaussian_sigma_norm between cells that survive and cells that die. Output is a printed table plus frame0_fate_comparison.csv with feature, n_survived, n_died, median_survived, median_died, U, p_value. Implementation: compare_frame0_features_by_fate() in src/cell_analysis/matching.py.
  2. Multivariate (second cell below). add_fate_prediction() fits a logistic regression on the same five features using leave-one-out cross-validation (appropriate for ~350 cells) and reports AUC, accuracy, and z-scored feature coefficients. Outputs: fate_predictions.csv (per-cell probability) and fate_prediction_summary.csv (single-row summary). Implementation: predict_fate_from_frame0() in src/cell_analysis/matching.py, plot in plot_fate_prediction() in src/cell_analysis/plotting.py.

The Mann-Whitney table tests each feature in isolation; the logistic regression asks whether the five together can rank cells by death probability (ROC curve + feature importance).

Related views of the same question, elsewhere in the report:

  • §8.17 Initial fluorescence features vs. lifespan — same frame-0 features, but plotted against the continuous lifetime variable with Spearman rho. Mann-Whitney here, Spearman there.
  • §6.5 Swelling extent vs. initial cell size and survival — initial volume vs. eventual fate (V(0) split by survived/disappeared).

Per-class diagnostics + feature-set comparison (Pass C). The cell now also prints the confusion matrix and per-class precision/recall/F1 — the 0.77/0.51 recall asymmetry the reviewer noticed on run_01 reappears in this output automatically. A second LR fit uses FATE_FEATURES_NO_AREA (the 4-feature set without area); both fits are saved to disk and a side-by-side comparison table is printed. If the no-area variant improves both per-class F1 by ≥ 0.02, swap FATE_FEATURES_FULL for FATE_FEATURES_NO_AREA in the Configuration cell for subsequent runs.

8.16 Nucleus persistence after cell lysis¶

Do fluorescent nuclei (DNA) survive as discrete objects after the cell membrane ruptures? To test this, we independently segment the fluorescence channel with Cellpose and compare object counts frame-by-frame against phase-contrast cells.

If nuclei persist after lysis, fluorescence counts should decline slower than phase counts (growing offset). If they disperse immediately, both should decline in parallel (constant offset).

Phase cells lost (first to last frame): 198
Fluor nuclei lost (first to last frame): 193
Difference std across frames: 7.7

Conclusion: Phase cells and fluorescent nuclei disappear at the same rate. DNA signal does NOT persist as a discrete object after cell lysis — the fluorescent material disperses upon membrane rupture.

Phase vs fluor count: Pearson r = 0.995, p = 6.42e-31

Sources: nucleus_persistence.csv, nucleus_persistence_summary.csv

8.17 Initial fluorescence features vs. lifespan¶

Do cells with different initial fluorescence states live longer? Scatter of frame-0 fluorescence intensity, CV, and nNRM against track lifetime, with Spearman rho printed per panel. Complements §8.14 Cell fate prediction, which tests the same three features against the binary survived/died split (Mann-Whitney + logistic regression). Lifetime here is the continuous outcome; fate there is the dichotomised one.

Implementation: plot_initial_features_vs_lifespan() in src/cell_analysis/plotting.py.

Initial fluorescence vs lifetime: Spearman rho = -0.086, p = 2.00e-01
Initial CV vs lifetime: Spearman rho = -0.105, p = 1.16e-01
Initial nNRM vs lifetime: Spearman rho = -0.181, p = 6.47e-03

Sources: tracked_cells.csv, track_statistics.csv

10. Export HTML Report¶

Saves the notebook to disk and exports a self-contained HTML copy to results/<RUN_NAME>/report.html. Set EXPORT_HTML = False (top of notebook) to skip. The CLI runner (scripts/run_experiment.py) uses the same exporter, so interactive and CLI reports stay in sync.
